title: Dongshan Suchness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk explores the idea that true understanding and freedom from suffering can't be found through words or explanations, but rather by looking within ourselves and embracing uncertainty. A story about Dongshan suggests that true freedom lies not in avoiding difficulties, but in understanding their nature, which is not separate from our own fundamental self. By examining our thoughts and perceptions, we can find contentment in the present moment and directly encounter reality, rather than trying to escape or avoid it.

sentences.text: Good evening.
Thanks for coming.
I really appreciate that we get to do our little choreography, different practices woven together.
Meditation is central to Zen practice, certainly, but it really exists in a kind of an ecosystem of being together—doing the walking and the chanting and standing in just such a way.
It's very community-based, everyone doing the same thing together.
So we somehow figured out how to get a lot in two hours without feeling too frantic or too rushed or anything like that.
We could just sit, but we have to do more.
Before I start my talk, I wanted to report back for those of us who weren't able to be at our eight-day retreat last week.
Every year in June, about the middle of June, we rent a church camp on Sandwich Island in the Skagit Valley from the Community of Christ, who are our good friends nowadays.
Our guiding teacher from California, Norman Fischer, is the lead teacher of the retreat, and we now just see him a couple of times a year.
It was very smooth this year, though it was a different experience for every person there because each of us brings ourselves along, and we have to deal with that.
It felt good to everybody, and Norman really appreciated it.
To file that away, we have it pretty worked out.

It's a little bit lost in the sands of time what year we first went there, but we've been going there every year since either ninety-five or ninety-six, making this the eighteenth or nineteenth annual retreat.
We'll figure out the exact year so we know when to celebrate the twentieth retreat next year or a year after.
There are three ways to be there; these retreats are pretty structured.
You sign up, and you are there for a certain part of it.
You can come to the entire thing, which is seven and a half days, eight nights, something like that.
Or you can come to half of it, which might be more manageable.
Or you can come down and just join the community for the Dharma talks in the morning and then slip out again, which a few people did.
It's always nice to have people come, and the talks were recorded and will be on the website in a couple of weeks once they unload the recorder in California.
That went well.
Some of you maybe were here instead last night, which I really appreciate.
That central element of this seems to be just showing up.
Maybe that's pretty much the whole thing—just showing up.
I think it's really great that we've managed to have people.
It's not always the same people, of course, but people just showing up at least once a week for quite a while in Bellingham to practice in this style.
Once in a while we've taken Thanksgiving off or something, but pretty much every week since the middle of nineteen ninety-one.
That's kind of great, so thanks for helping us not skip a week if you're one of those people.
I want to try to say a little something tonight about the Buddhist teaching called suchness.

Suchness is an idea that doesn't have a very good analog in English, like many of the rich ideas that especially the Mahayana, the sort of second major wave of Buddhist thought, brought to world culture; not all of it translates very well.
So I want to start out with an American nature poem, and then we'll have some Zen stories to try to think a little bit about this idea of suchness—things being such, being just as they are.
This is Mary Oliver's "The Summer Day."
*Who made the world?
Who made the swan and the black bear?
Who made the grasshopper?

This grasshopper, I mean, the one who has flung herself out of the grass, the one who was eating sugar out of my hand, who was moving her jaws back and forth instead of up and down, who was gazing around with her enormous and complicated eyes.
Now she lifts her pale forearms and thoroughly washes her face.
Now she snaps her wings open and floats away.
I don't know exactly what a prayer is.
I do know how to pay attention.
How to fall down into the grass.
How to kneel down in the grass.
How to be idle and blessed.
How to stroll through the fields, which is what I have been doing all day.
Tell me, what else should I have done?
Doesn't everything die at last and too soon?
What is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?*
"The Summer Day," Mary Oliver.
Who made the world?
Who made the swan and the black bear?
Who made the grasshopper?

This grasshopper, I mean, the one who has flung herself out of the grass, the one who was eating sugar out of my hand, who was moving her jaws back and forth instead of up and down, who was gazing around with her enormous and complicated eyes.
Now she lifts her pale forearms and thoroughly washes her face.
Now she snaps her wings open and floats away.
I don't know exactly what a prayer is.
I do know how to pay attention.
How to fall down into the grass.
How to kneel down in the grass.
How to be idle and blessed.
How to stroll through the fields, which is what I have been doing all day.
Tell me, what else should I have done?
Doesn't everything die at last and too soon?
Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"
That's pretty good, huh?
My favorite line currently is, "Tell me, what else should I have done?"
You could also think of this as a conversation with yourself, right?
There's so much to do, time to hang around and lying around in the fields.
When was the last time that you hung around lying around in the field all day?
They have many different names for the Buddha to try to, on the one hand, really express some sense of appreciation or reverence, if you will.
You have lots of complementary positive names for the Buddha.

On the other hand, as a way to sort of explore the different dimensions of what it might mean—what might it be to be Buddha, to be awakened, to be in some way fully actualizing the possibility of being a human being.
There are lots of different names, and one of the names I want to focus on tonight is in one of our chants, I think, the chant right before the talk.
Good.
That is Tathagata, Tathagata.
The first part of that, tata, tata, is this suchness I want to talk about tonight.
The gatha part is like a being, person, or a one.
So that nickname for the Buddha means the one who is just such, or sometimes they translate it as the one who thus comes.
Something about just being here, just showing up.
Back to our emphasis and practice here: just showing up.
Not like waiting until we're like, you know, got our head straight or are calm or going to impress somebody, but just showing up, just being what and who we are in this moment.
This is a little hard to talk about because language has an inherent quality of dividing things, dividing things into categories, which we need in order to function.
That's why they talk about being dualistic.

Sometimes dualistic sounds like a bad thing or something wrong with you if you're dualistic, but it's just natural to be dualistic because nothing can really function in the conventional world without dualism, without this or that, or this and that.
The word big doesn't actually have any meaning unless you have small, right?
And the reverse.
Things exist in relationship to each other, and so they need some way to look at each other.
You can't look at each other unless you're in some way separated.
This creates a powerful and complicated world in which many things are possible and there are many problems—this world of this or that, me or you.
This suchness is a quality of being that somehow drops, rises over this dividing, or maybe flows through both divisions of every category equally without hindrance.
Since it's so hard to talk about in a descriptive or discursive way, sometimes poetry, sometimes stories of encounter.

Zen is famous for these stories of people encountering each other and trying to feel into the broader dimensions of our living that can't always be described, couldn't put them on the curriculum or write a book about them exactly.
So they wrote thousands and thousands of books about it.
Some of them stories that were told and later written down, some of them stories that were written down, some stories that were written down with the fiction that they were told earlier.
But luckily many survived the ages.

We have this large collection of stories of people cooperating together or challenging each other in some way to leap free from the ways that we can imprison or cripple ourselves because we feel a little inadequate now.
Why do we feel inadequate?

Because our incredibly powerful minds can imagine some fantasy other version of ourselves, in some fantasy other version of reality in which there is something different or improved, or at least there should be something different or improved if we can't quite think what it should be.
These are encounters of people, Zen practitioners in this case, encouraging each other to just drop in to the suchness of their life.
I want to tell you a story, a series of stories about a Zen teacher from China, eighth century, yes, eighth century, named Dongshan.
Norman mentioned him in one of the stories this last week; Norman mentioned several times last week if you were there, Dongshan's teacher named Yunyan.
It's a little ecosystem of stories, kind of true and kind of wonderfully invented too.

Dongshan had studied for a long time with his teacher Yunyan, and it's not totally clear, but maybe he was getting ready to sort of had completed his studies and was getting ready to leave Yunyan's monastery.
Junsheng asked a question: "After your death, teacher, if someone asked me if I can describe your teaching, how shall I reply?
In other words, how should I remember you?
After your death, if someone asked me how to describe your teaching or your reality, how should I reply?"
Yunyan said, "Just this is it.
Just this is it."
So suchness, just this is it.
Dongshan sank into thought.
Whoa, just this is it.
And Yunyan looked at him and said, "You are in charge of this great matter.
You must be most thorough going.
You are in charge of this great matter.
You must be most thorough going."
So a little strong encouragement, you know, you need to understand what I'm telling you here because you're in charge.
Dongshan left without saying anything more.
Later, as he was crossing a river—this is a famous moment in Zen history—he was crossing a river, like a little log maybe, rivers moving slowly.
He looked down and saw his reflection.
In that moment he had a great realization, and later he composed this verse:
*Just don't seek from others or you'll be far estranged from it.
I now go on alone and everywhere I meet it.
It is now me.
I am not it.*
One must understand in this way to merge with suchness.
Don't seek, don't just seek from others or you'll be far estranged from it.
I now go on alone.
Everywhere I meet it.
It now is me.
I now am not it.
Not is interesting, huh?
What?
One must understand in this way to merge with suchness.
Clearly from the story, we need the support of others, teachers.
There are also many stories in here of peers; it's not always this sort of stereotypical master and disciple.
It seems like it's clearly framed that we need the support of others and the teachings of others, right?
So Dongshan presumably had studied with Yunyan and other teachers as well for many years.
But then his verse says don't just seek from others or you'll be estranged, but push yourself away from your own understanding.
There's something in us, something already there, something already understood, and a sense of really being comfortable in our own skin, right?
I now go on alone, and yet not alone.
Everywhere I meet it, I see it.
It is me.
I am not it.
Sometimes they say I'm trying to describe this kind of stuff—not one, not two, not one, not two.
This is something because sometimes we say in philosophy or religion there's like oneness, merging and oneness.
This is a little more subtle than that; even oneness is sort of like a category, which means there's not oneness.
So this is like sort of beyond oneness, not oneness, not just one, not separate.
They often use a lot of negation to try to describe this teaching, and that it's important; he says you have to understand to merge, to merge with suchness.
Later on, when Dongshan was a teacher himself, he told this story to try to teach his own students something about this topic of just being such.
He was presenting offerings before a picture of his teacher, Yunyan; it was maybe like a memorial service.
You would usually have a monthly memorial service for your root teacher on the day of the month that they died, which I suppose once Norman dies we'll start doing.
He retold the story about depicting Yunyan's teaching, his reality, and a monk came forward and said, "When Yunyan said, 'Just this is it,' what did he mean?"
Dongshan said to his student, "At that time I nearly misunderstood my late master."
The monk asked, "Did Yun Yang himself know it or not?"
A little impudent, Dung Shun replied, "If he didn't know, if he didn't know it is, how would he be able to say what he said?
If he did know it is, how would he be willing to say anything?"
That's the end of the second story, so the story is going to feed on itself.
We're batting something around here, and in a way these stories are frustrating because we have a way that we want to understand stories and make sense of things.

It might be that these kinds of stories and this odd way of talking—and this is of course translated from Chinese, which can make it a little hard—but I think even in the original Chinese it's a little odd.
A contemporary Chinese person would be like, "Huh?"

But it may be that something about this way of talking and thinking just softens or inclines our mind to be sensitive to some possibilities of understanding our life that aren't just bound by the narrative.
Like a sort of seeing of something out of the corner of our eye, or in a quiet moment, like when we're lying in the field all day to really see a grasshopper.
You can't really see a grasshopper if you're busy worrying about your job, right?
You just won't see it.
Literally, you won't notice that that grasshopper has landed in your hand, or you'll just be like, "Yeah."
Right?
The poet didn't do that.
She's like, "Oh wow, look at this."
And that's the quality that these stories have also.
Look at this, even though they're using very abstract and strange language, using the word "it" or "this."
So the monks said, "Did Yun Yang understand this?
What he was telling you?"
And Dongshan says basically, "Well, it's not exactly about understanding or not understanding; it's a different thing than that.
If he didn't know, how would he be able to say anything?
If he did know, why would he say anything?"
So how do you understand your life?
How do you talk about your life to yourself, to others?
Is what you say about your life really true, or is it really not true?
If you really understood your life, would you say anything about it, or would you not say anything about it?
Another time Dongshan said to the monks in his monastery, "It's the beginning of autumn, the end of summer.
And you, brethren, will go.
Some to the east, some to the west.
You must go where there's not an inch of grass for 10,000 miles."
He also said, "But where there's not an inch of grass for 10,000 miles, how can you go?"
Xishuang, one of the students, said, "Going out the gate, immediately there is grass."
Dayang, another one, said, "I say, even not going out the gate, still the grass is boundless."
So grass here is code for just reality, meaning all things are like grass, just growing everywhere and all the things in the universe.
The framing of the story is always kind of coded.

The way we're supposed to understand this is they would have a summer and a winter training period, like an intensive three-month training period where all the monks and nuns would live a very intense schedule and stay in the monastery.
Then in the fall and the spring, they'd have a lighter time, and the monks could travel.
The monks and nuns could travel, maybe go visit another monastery, maybe go home or something.
So it's sort of like we have to turn around.
For us, it would be like it's the end of graduation, and you're all leaving for the summer or something like that.
So he's saying many of you are going to travel.
Where do you think you're going?
Where do you think you're really going?
Do you think you're going east or do you think you're going west?
But you really need to go where there's not an inch of grass for 10,000 miles.
You really need to understand that the way you see reality isn't quite how it is.
Things are not the way you think, is kind of what he's saying.
The real reality is hard to understand, as if there's nothing and everything.

But where there's not an inch of grass for 10,000 miles, if you understand the unknowableness of reality, if you understand that things are much deeper and more subtle than our names and visions and memories and concepts, if you understand that there's not grass or anything you can grab onto, how can you go anywhere?
How can you go?
We have two different student answers, and we don't have a response from the teacher, so we are to assume that these are probably pretty good answers.
One said, "Going out the gate, immediately there's grass."
So that is, "Even though I don't understand, I'm going to take a step forward.
I'm going to enter into my life with a good spirit.
And I'll see what is with the truest eyes, that I have.
I'll see the grass, but I have to do something."
That's like a pretty good answer.
And then the next one is supposed to be a little better answer.
The second guy says, "I assume they're probably both men.
I'd say, even not going out the gate, still, the grass is boundless.
Things are not bound by our view of them."
One more story of Dongshan.
Dongshan, by the way, his name, the Japanese have another way of pronouncing these Chinese characters, so it gets confusing because there's all these names.
Each individual person had multiple different names and different parts of their career too, but the Japanese name for this character, Dongshan, is Tozan.
Tozan, and that he is the To in Soto.
So Soto Zen is our school of Zen.
So Dongshan or Tozan is one of the founders, which is kind of a looking backwards way of sending founder.
He had no idea he was founding a school of Zen in Japan, but later they decided that was the case.
This is probably the most famous story of Dongshan.
The monasteries were not super comfortable places.
Not a lot of heat and definitely no air conditioning in 8th century China.
It can be pretty hot.
A monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat come, how can we avoid them?
Or how can we deal with them?"
Dongshan said, "Well, why don't you go to a place where there is no cold or heat?
Why don't you go to a place where there is no cold or heat?"
The monk said, "What is the place where there is no cold or heat?"
Dongshan said, "When it's cold, the cold kills you.
When it's hot, the heat kills you."
That's the end of the story.
This is a great story about all kinds of things, preferences, comfort seeking.
And here is duality, right?
Cold and heat, language, using language to divide things.
And how much of our discomfort at things that we do not like is based on our language, our talking to ourselves about it, our anticipating, our thinking about the future.
"I can no way, I can withstand this.
This is going to go on much longer, right?"
It's kind of an odd thing to say, like, "Well, how would you know?"
It makes me think of when I went to the dentist on Tuesday, and I had this kind of chronic thing going on where the gums receded for some reason.
Anyway, you don't need to know all about my teeth.
I'm getting periodically these very small cavities, and the dentist watches it for a while, and then I have to get a small filling.
I've done several of these.
It doesn't matter how good I brush; this is going to happen.
So I have an agreement with the dentist.
He knows I'm a meditator and all this, and I've been seeing him for a long time.
I have an agreement with him not to have the anesthetic because it's just more impact on your day to getting numb and drooling and all this stuff.
Really, I'm not trying to show off; it's just easier for me, I think.
I'm going to try to show off a little bit.
I mean, you know, it's all cool.
But the dental assistant who's helping with the operation, they've got to drill out, they've got to clean out the part that's a little bit decayed and put the filling in.
She had never heard of such a thing, somebody getting a filling and not having the anesthetic, and so she was kind of alarmed and had to check it out with him.
It was interesting, too.
She was like sort of studying me through the whole procedure and talking about what I was doing.
Very well-meaning, but as if I wasn't there.
She's like, "Wow, he seems like he's not really moving his eyes.
Maybe he's just kind of goes somewhere.
Dr.
Scott's just kind of working away.
She's handing him instruments and just kind of."
I'm convinced not that I'm a world champion meditator and I can enter like a health, self-hypnotic state and not notice the pain.
I can feel the discomfort of it.

But I'm convinced that it's the thought of it, that's the most difficult for us, the thought of choosing discomfort, or choosing pain, and that it's really almost impossible for us to unpack the sensation from the thought, the fear, the projection, the future, the past, all the things that are happening in the mind.
So, when the dental drill comes, you want to go someplace where there's no dental drill.
"Yes, please."
There's nothing wrong if you get anesthetic.
It's good to get anesthetic, you know.
But how does the mind create reality—hot, cold, dental drill, everything else?
Our actual founder in Japan, maybe he did have a sense of founding something.
Dogen really liked this story.
I might just go over a couple of minutes to read you what Dogen said about this, then we'll stop.
I also want to read you his comment on it.
The translator of this section of Dogen used slightly different words to translate the actual story, which is interesting too because Chinese characters have lots of shades of meaning.
So this is from a chapter, the beginning of a chapter in Dogen's great work, *Shobogenzo*.
*Dongshan, great master Wuben, was once asked by a monk, "When cold or heat comes, how can we avoid it?"
Dongshan said, "One should go where there is no cold or heat."
The monk said, "What do you mean by where there is no cold or heat?"
Dongshan said, "When it is cold, cold finishes the monk.
When it is hot, heat demolishes the monk."*
So different from kill.
This is all Dogen quoting, and now Dogen comments.
This story has often been examined in the past.
Many of you should now also pursue it now.
Buddha ancestors have never failed to master this matter.
And those who have mastered it are Buddha ancestors.
Buddha ancestors in India and China, past and present, often made this issue the face and eye of their realization.
To bring forth this face and eye is the fundamental point of Buddha Dharma.
This being so, examine in detail the monk's question: "When cold or heat comes, how can we avoid it?"
This is the study of the very moment when cold comes or the very moment when heat comes.
This cold or heat, complete cold or complete heat, is itself cold or heat.
Accordingly, when either comes, it comes from the summit of cold, like the mountaintop, the summit of heat, and manifests from the eyeball of cold itself and the eyeball of heat itself.
This summit is where there is no cold or heat.
This eyeball is where there is no cold or heat.
Dogen's words, "When it is cold, cold finishes the monk.
When it is hot, heat demolishes the monk."
Show how it is when the moment arrives.
Even if there is the expression, "When it is cold, cold finishes," it is not necessary that when it is hot, heat demolishes the expression.
Cold penetrates the root of cold.
Heat penetrates the root of heat.
Even if you try millions of times to avoid cold and heat, it is like trying to put a tail where the head is.
Cold is the vital eyeball of the ancestral school.
Heat is the warm skin and flesh of my late master, which is like the most superlative thing you can imagine to say.
This is as good as my late master.
We can talk more about cold and heat later, but just some stories around this theme of suchness, things just as they are in a world where we create so many limitations with our language.
I'll close with a really short poem, and we'll stop for real.
*This is Ryokan, an early 18th century Japanese monk-poet.
"I don't regard my life as insufficient.
Inside the brushwood gate there is a moon.
There are flowers."
That's the whole poem.
"I don't regard my life as insufficient.
Inside the brushwood gate there is a moon.
There are flowers."
That's enough, in other words.*
